family_lesson.where_to_look_first: Find an areole. It is the strongest structural family cue: a specialized axillary structure that can produce spines, glochids, hairs, branches and flowers. Then read stem segmentation/ribs/tubercles, leaf reduction, flower position, inferior ovary and berry-like fruit.
authoritative_framework: Succulent perennial habit is common but growth form varies widely.
Areoles are the defining high-value structural cue and originate spines, hairs, branches and flowers.
Leaves are often highly reduced or absent in mature plants.
Flowers usually have many perianth segments and many stamens.
Ovary is inferior; fruit is typically berry-like and many-seeded.
Spines may be absent in some family members, so do not make spines mandatory.
opuntia_layer: Flattened or cylindrical segmented stems are cladodes/stem segments, not ordinary leaves.
Opuntioideae adds barbed glochids at the areoles.
Use pad/segment form, areole spacing, glochid/spine pattern, flower and fruit for local Opuntia comparisons.
avoid_overgeneralizing: Do not identify Cactaceae from succulence alone.
Do not require obvious large spines.
Do not teach flattened pads as a family-wide character.
Do not call the pad a leaf.
Do not count Opuntia lindheimeri separately from accepted Opuntia engelmannii var. lindheimeri in current Kew taxonomy.

confusable_families.Euphorbiaceae: Succulent Euphorbia can mimic cactus form, but lacks true cactus areoles; flowers/inflorescences are fundamentally different.
confusable_families.Asparagaceae: Agave/Yucca can look spiny and drought-adapted from a distance, but they retain true leaves in a rosette and lack cactus areoles.
